questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Two masses linked by a spring on a smooth surface
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a joined pair of masses oscillates while sliding on a smooth surface.
questions.stem: Brief clause on the twin-panel damper describes two identical 0.50 kg panels joined by a 200 N/m spring on a smooth floor. Explain, using the relative motion, how the pair oscillates.

answer.exemplar: For two equal masses m joined by a spring k on a smooth floor, m times the acceleration of the first equals -k times the difference of the positions and likewise for the second, so subtracting gives m times the second derivative of the separation equal to -2k times the separation. The relative motion therefore oscillates at angular frequency sqrt(2k/m), here sqrt(800) = 28.3 rad per second, while the centre of mass has no net force on it and drifts at constant speed, the spring supplying all the energy of the vibration.

questions.explanation: The separation obeys m times its second derivative equal to -2k times itself, so the relative frequency is sqrt(2k/m), here 28.3 rad per second. The centre of mass drifts at constant speed.
questions.hint: Separate the relative motion from the centre of mass.

questions.topic: Two masses linked by a spring on a smooth surface
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a joined pair can slide while still vibrating.
questions.stem: Brief appendix on the isolation deck describes two 1.0 kg masses linked by a 300 N/m spring on a smooth surface. Explain why the pair can slide while still vibrating.

answer.exemplar: With no friction on the deck the only horizontal forces are internal spring forces, which cancel for the pair taken as a whole, so the centre of mass moves at constant velocity. The spring still acts between the masses, so the difference of their positions obeys m times its second derivative equal to -2k times that difference, giving relative oscillation at angular frequency sqrt(2k/m) = sqrt(600) = 24.5 rad per second. The pair therefore translates freely while the spring stores and returns the energy of the relative vibration.

questions.explanation: The translation of the centre of mass and the stretching of the spring are independent motions, so sliding and vibrating happen at the same time. A stretched spring does not stop the pair from moving.
questions.hint: The centre of mass and the separation behave separately.

questions.topic: Two masses linked by a spring on a smooth surface
questions.learningObjective: Explain where the energy of the vibration of a joined pair is stored.
questions.stem: Brief clause on the acoustic isolator asks why the vibration energy of a joined pair stays in the spring while the pair slides along the floor.

answer.exemplar: On a smooth surface no net external horizontal force acts on the pair, so the centre of mass moves at constant speed and none of the energy sits in the translation. The vibration is entirely in the relative motion of the two masses, whose separation obeys m times its second derivative equal to -2k times the separation. The spring stores half k times the square of its extension and returns that energy each cycle, so the oscillation persists while the pair slides on without any friction to stop it.

questions.explanation: The translation carries no energy on a frictionless floor, so all the vibration energy sits in the stretched spring. The idea that sliding drains the vibration confuses the two independent motions.
questions.hint: On a smooth floor the centre of mass keeps a constant speed.

answer.exemplar: For two equal masses m joined by a spring k, subtracting the two equations of motion gives m times the second derivative of the separation equal to -2k times the separation, so the relative frequency is the square root of 2k over m. Doubling each mass therefore divides the frequency by the square root of two, while the centre of mass still slides at constant speed. The tempting idea that the vibration frequency is fixed by the spring alone misses that the effective mass of the relative motion is two masses sharing the restoring work.

questions.explanation: The relative motion sees twice the spring constant and one member as its effective mass, so the frequency falls with the square root of the mass. A frequency set by the spring alone ignores inertia.
questions.hint: The separation sees twice the spring stiffness.

questions.topic: Two masses linked by a spring on a smooth surface
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a coupled pair can move while the spring keeps a constant length.
questions.stem: Brief note on the laboratory mount describes two panels joined by a spring on a smooth table and asks why the spring extension can stay constant while the panels move.

answer.exemplar: The two masses move apart and back with a fixed separation in the sliding mode, because in that pattern the spring keeps a constant length and so exerts no force while the centre of mass coasts along at constant speed. The relative vibration is a separate mode, in which the spring stretches and compresses and the separation obeys m times its second derivative equal to -2k times the separation. questions.explanation: A constant spring length with the panels moving is exactly the sliding mode, in which the spring is unstrained and the pair coasts. A stretched spring is not needed for any motion.
questions.hint: Look for the mode in which the spring is not strained.
